principles.name: Users first
principles.description: Put the needs and trust of the businesses and developers who depend on Stripe ahead of everything else.
evidence_signals: Names the specific user (developer, merchant, finance team) and their pain
Treats reliability and trust as user features
Changed a plan after talking to users

principles.name: Create with craft and beauty
principles.description: Approach work with care and high standards so the result is excellent, including the parts no one sees.
evidence_signals: Talks about quality of code, docs, API design or writing, not only shipping
Describes polishing details that improved the user experience
Explains a quality bar they held and why

principles.name: Move with urgency and focus
principles.description: Execute quickly on what matters most while still investing in long-term improvements.
evidence_signals: Shows clear prioritization and saying no to lower-value work
Ships iteratively with a short feedback loop
Balances speed with long-term health of the system

principles.name: Collaborate egolessly
principles.description: Work as one team: question assumptions, debate openly, and drop an idea when a better one appears.
evidence_signals: Describes abandoning own idea for a better one
Handles disagreement on substance, not status

principles.name: Stay curious
principles.description: Keep learning about how businesses and the world work, and go deep on unfamiliar problems.
evidence_signals: Shows genuine interest in payments, economics or the user's business
Describes learning a new domain fast to solve a problem

principles.name: Obsess over talent
principles.description: Everyone owns hiring and raising the bar; push for high standards across the organization.
evidence_signals: Describes interviewing, mentoring or developing others
Gives an example of raising the bar on a team
Makes a clear, hard people decision

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background and fit. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.notes: Written exercise reflecting a real problem; Stripe weights written communication heavily. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.notes: Design, improvement and strategy prompts, often about payments, APIs or e-commerce.

rounds.name: Technical depth
rounds.notes: Explain and defend technical and API design choices.

rounds.name: Execution and behavioral
rounds.notes: Behavioral depth on shipping, prioritization and ambiguity.

question_patterns.pattern: A mistake the candidate made while leading something big, and how they fixed it
A time the candidate insisted on a higher quality bar, and what it cost and gained
A recent time the candidate said no to something in order to focus on what mattered
A disagreement where the candidate debated openly and the better idea won, whoever owned it
A product or system the candidate is proud of: the user, own role, decisions and result
How the candidate hires, grows or raises the bar for the people around them
How the candidate makes progress when the problem and goals are unclear
Design a developer-facing API and its backend, with idempotency, versioning and error semantics
Design a system where money must never be lost or double counted (ledger, billing, reconciliation)
Walk through how a service behaves under partial failure, retries and dependency outages

question_patterns.theme: Product design for a new user group
question_patterns.pattern: Design a product for an unusual user group and justify the core experience
Step into a leader's role and choose the few things that matter most for a business
Define the right metrics for a business or experience and what to watch daily

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a mistake you made while leading a significant project. How did you fix it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a real, consequential mistake that was yours. Explain context, how you noticed, the impact on users or the team, and the concrete fix. Show egoless behavior: you surfaced it quickly, did not blame others, and accepted better ideas. End with the process change you made. Stripe interviewers value candour and learning. Pitfall: a minor or blame-shifting example.

sample_questions.question: When did you last say no to a request or idea, and why?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a recent, specific case where saying no was hard (a senior stakeholder, a customer, a teammate). Explain how you weighed it against priorities, how you communicated the no with reasoning and an alternative, and what happened. Shows focus and respectful directness. Pitfall: a trivial no, or one with no reasoning.

sample_questions.question: How do you work when a problem is highly ambiguous? Give an example.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe a real ambiguous situation and your method: clarify the goal, list unknowns, talk to users or experts, pick a small step to learn fast, and write down decisions. Show curiosity about the domain and how you converged on a direction quickly. Mention how you kept stakeholders aligned. Pitfall: generic framework talk with no example.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you held a high quality bar when others wanted to ship sooner.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain what 'quality' meant concretely (correctness, API ergonomics, docs, performance) and why it mattered to users. Show how you made the case, what trade-off you agreed (scope cut, phased launch) and the outcome. Stripe looks for craft balanced with urgency, so acknowledge the cost of delay. Pitfall: perfectionism with no user reason.

sample_questions.question: Describe a conflict with a colleague and how it was resolved.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a substantive disagreement. Show you stated your view, sought theirs, tested assumptions with data or a prototype, and supported the better idea even if it was not yours. Describe the outcome and the relationship afterwards. Egoless collaboration is the core signal. Pitfall: framing the other person as the problem.

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a product or system you delivered that you are most proud of.
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the user problem, your specific role, the key design or product decisions and trade-offs, and the result with numbers. Point out a detail of craft (API shape, docs, reliability) that made a difference to users. Hiring managers calibrate scope from this, so be clear about team size and your influence. Pitfall: describing the team's work without your part.

sample_questions.question: As a manager, tell me about a strategic hiring decision you made and how it played out.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the team need, how you defined the role and bar, how you evaluated candidates, and a hard call (waiting longer, rejecting a strong but wrong-fit candidate, hiring for potential). Describe results and what you learned. Stripe expects everyone to own talent. Pitfall: hiring to fill a seat quickly with no bar.

sample_questions.question: Why are you looking to leave your current role, and why Stripe?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be positive and specific: what you want next (scope, domain, craft) and why Stripe's problems in payments and developer infrastructure fit. Show curiosity about how money moves on the internet and knowledge of a Stripe product. Pitfall: complaining about the current employer.

sample_questions.question: Design a ledger service that records money movements for a payments platform.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify requirements: immutability, double-entry, auditability, multi-currency, query patterns. Propose append-only entries, balanced transactions, idempotent writes, and derived balances with snapshots. Discuss consistency (strong for writes), reconciliation with external processors, corrections via reversing entries, and scaling by account sharding. Stripe values correctness and failure handling over buzzwords.

sample_questions.question: Design an API rate limiter for a public API.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define limits per key or account and the response contract (status code, headers, retry-after). Compare token bucket, sliding window and fixed window. Discuss a distributed counter store, accuracy versus latency, and what happens when the store is slow or down (fail open or closed, local fallback). Mention observability and how developers understand they are throttled.

sample_questions.question: Design a metrics service that collects and serves operational metrics.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify writers, cardinality and query needs. Cover ingestion with batching, time-series storage with downsampling and retention, aggregation, and a query API. Discuss high-cardinality labels, late data, and keeping the metrics pipeline more available than what it monitors. Explain trade-offs clearly with numbers.

sample_questions.question: Design a payment processing API and the system behind it, considering how developers will integrate with it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Treat the API as a product: resources, states (created, authorized, captured, refunded), idempotency keys so retries are safe, clear error types, versioning and backward compatibility. Then the internal workflow: async calls to card networks, partial failures, webhooks for state changes, and the ledger. Discuss how developers observe what happened. Strong answers balance internal correctness and external predictability.

sample_questions.question: How would you design reliable webhook delivery when merchants' servers are sometimes slow or down?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover an event log, a delivery queue per endpoint, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, at-least-once semantics with event IDs so receivers can deduplicate, signatures for authenticity, ordering caveats, and disabling or alerting on persistently failing endpoints. Explain how a bad endpoint is isolated so it cannot slow others. Mention a dashboard for developers to replay events.

sample_questions.question: In your view, what makes an API good?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give principles with examples: consistent naming and resources, predictable errors, idempotency, sensible defaults, versioning without breaking users, excellent docs and examples, and observability. Tie each to developer trust and time to integrate. Contrast with an API you found painful. Pitfall: listing REST rules without a user perspective.

sample_questions.question: How would you approach detecting fraud in a payments product?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Frame the trade-off between blocking fraud and blocking good customers, and that both cost merchants. Cover signals (device, velocity, card history, network-wide patterns), a rules plus model approach, real-time scoring latency, feedback from disputes, and letting merchants tune thresholds. Discuss metrics like false positive rate and dispute rate.

sample_questions.question: If you were Stripe's CEO, what would be your top three priorities?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show you understand Stripe's business: who pays, how revenue grows, competition and risks. Pick three priorities with clear reasoning and trade-offs (what you would not do). Tie each to user needs and a way to measure progress. Strong answers are focused and opinionated, not a laundry list.

sample_questions.question: Design a communication product for young children.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify age range and the buyers versus users (parents versus kids). Identify needs and constraints: safety, privacy, literacy, parental control. Brainstorm, prioritize one core experience, sketch it, and define success metrics and risks. Interviewers want user empathy and fast but intentional decisions. Pitfall: ignoring safety and the parent as customer.

sample_questions.question: What metrics should Stripe look at every day?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Organize by goal: health of the business (payment volume, revenue, new accounts), user trust (API availability, latency, authorization rate, dispute rate), and growth (activation of new integrations). Explain why each matters, what would trigger action, and avoid vanity metrics. Discuss leading versus lagging indicators.

sample_questions.question: How would you measure customer satisfaction with airport baggage claim?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the user journey and what satisfaction means (wait time, uncertainty, lost bags). Propose a north-star metric and supporting metrics (time to first bag, variance, mishandling rate, survey score), how to collect them, and guardrails. Explain trade-offs between measurability and what users feel. Concise structure wins.

sample_questions.question: You run product at a struggling retail chain with physical stores and no online presence. What would you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Diagnose before prescribing: why it struggles, customers, margins, strengths of stores. Consider options (e-commerce, buy online pick up in store, inventory visibility) and prioritize by impact, cost and time. Propose a phased plan with metrics. Strong answers connect to payments and commerce infrastructure realistically.

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Works on defined tasks within one team with supervision. Title: Software Engineer.
Owns complete features within a team and reviews peers' work independently. Title: Software Engineer.
Decides what should be built and drives work across team boundaries; the step to L3 is about scope. Title still Software Engineer.
Staff Software Engineer; sets technical direction for an organizational area and leads multiple teams.
Senior Staff Software Engineer; leads technical strategy across a large group.

persona.tone: Thoughtful, precise and low-ego; values clear written-style communication
persona.pace: Measured; gives room to reason but expects crisp, well-structured answers
persona.pushback_style: Probes failure modes, edge cases and user impact ('what happens if this call is retried?', 'how does the developer know?'), and asks the candidate to justify trade-offs
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for questions and welcomes curious questions about Stripe's users and business

case_style.notes: Product cases range from playful design prompts to Stripe strategy and metrics; systems thinking about APIs, payments and developer experience runs through them. Classic market-sizing is rare.

sources.title: How I would approach the Stripe system design interview today

low_confidence_notes: loop_structure: rounds come from prep guides and candidate reports; Stripe does not publish its loop. The Glassdoor report was only seen as a search result, not opened. PM levels are not public, so the PM loop lists no levels.
bar_by_level: level names L1-L5 and scope come from one third-party guide; Stripe job posts show only three titles. No PM level data.
case_style: few PM case reports; weights estimated.
scoring_weights: estimated from the operating principles and reports that stress clean code, writing and failure handling.
